clue.text: There's nothing to pay if one can get on it

definitions.text: There's nothing to pay if one can get on it

parts.words: There's nothing to pay if one can get on it
parts.note: describes a roster of people admitted without charge, such as guests let into a theatre for nothing

explanation.definitionFit: A roster of people allowed in without paying, so getting onto it means paying nothing.

clue.text: An assembly after medical treatment?

definitions.meaning: a mechanic who puts together machine parts
healthier, as one should be once treated

explanation.definitionFit: A mechanic who puts parts together, and the comparative of healthy, describing a patient after a cure.

clue.text: Extremely 000 verse love love

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads 'Extremely 000 verse love love (4,2)': '000' is garbled and 'love' is doubled, so the anagram indicator before 'verse' is missing

clue.text: Tiny raised inlay that may have to be made up

definitions.text: that may have to be made up

indicators.note: the turned word goes inside the other piece

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down clue raising a word turns it upside down, so it is read from the bottom

parts.note: wee is Scottish and informal for tiny

explanation.surface: A small decorative inset is lifted out and must be repaired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inlay' looks like decorative work but splits as 'in' (the container signal) and 'lay'; 'raised' suits a down clue, where the word is read upwards. Leeway to make up is lost time or ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Lost time or ground is something you must catch up on, as in making up leeway.

clue.text: Nicknames for the blocks of coal-dust they use at the Stationery Office?

parts.note: SO is short for the Stationery Office, the British government publisher
briquets are compressed blocks of coal dust used as fuel

explanation.surface: A joke about the fuel burnt at the government printing office.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stationery Office (HMSO) is the British government's official publisher and printer; its abbreviation goes in front of the fuel blocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Familiar or playful names given to people in place of real ones.

clue.text: A warning now pointless, apparently

definitions.meaning: a confidential hint or alert given in advance
read as two words, something whose tip has come off has lost its point

explanation.definitionFit: A private alert is a hint given in advance; read literally, the phrase describes an object with its point removed.

clue.text: A god that will never be forgotten

definitions.meaning: a deity, one who never dies
remembered for ever, of undying fame

explanation.definitionFit: A deathless deity, and an adjective for fame that lasts for ever.

clue.text: Cook too much food, maybe?

parts.note: 'cook too much' looks like preparing excess food, but means applying too much heat, which is what burning a dish involves

explanation.definitionFit: Cooking food for too long or too fiercely makes it too hot, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Charge that never varies for an apartment

definitions.meaning: a fixed fee that stays the same whatever the use
read literally, the local tax levied on an apartment

explanation.walkthrough: Rates were the British local tax on property, so this phrase also reads as the tax on a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed uniform price, and read literally the rates (British local property tax) on an apartment.

clue.text: Among our most popular annual events of course

definitions.text: Among our most popular annual events of course

parts.words: Among our most popular annual events of course
parts.note: 'of course' seems to mean 'naturally' but points to a racecourse, here Epsom's famous flat race held every June

explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' reads as 'naturally'; it is the racecourse. Epsom is a racecourse in Surrey, England, and its classic flat race draws huge crowds each year.
explanation.definitionFit: The Epsom race run each June is one of Britain's best-loved yearly sporting fixtures, held on a racecourse.

clue.text: The lowest form of life

parts.note: a single-celled organism, traditionally cited as the most primitive living creature

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is also an insult for a despicable person, which makes the solver think of people rather than biology.
explanation.definitionFit: A single-celled protozoan is the classic example of the simplest living organism.

clue.text: A suet pudding divided by a Channel Islands girl

indicators.note: the mixed letters are split apart by another piece placed between them
a pudding is a mixture of ingredients, so the letters of the preceding words are mixed up

explanation.surface: A suet pudding is being shared out by a young woman from Jersey or Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pudding' makes EUSTA, and 'divided by' splits it from the second A with the Channel Islands' letters. The Channel Islands lie off Normandy and belong to the British Crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A female first name, borne by Hardy's heroine in The Return of the Native.

clue.text: Comparatively roguish mediaeval soldier?

definitions.meaning: arch means mischievous or roguish, so its comparative form means more roguish
a bowman, the longbow being the typical weapon of medieval infantry

explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of arch (playfully mischievous) and a bowman of the Middle Ages share one spelling.

clue.text: Currently the way things are going

definitions.text: Currently the way things are going

parts.words: Currently the way things are going
parts.note: 'Currently' seems to mean 'at present' but means 'by the current', the direction a river carries things

explanation.definitionFit: Floating objects are carried by a river's current towards its mouth, in that direction.

clue.text: Pretend to provide the audience with a bit of variety

definitions.meaning: to feign or put up a false show

definitions.text: provide the audience with a bit of variety
definitions.meaning: to stage a turn in a variety show for spectators

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means feigning a manner; literally it means staging a turn for a music-hall audience.

clue.text: Wandering bear resorting to bombast

indicators.note: read as re-sorting, the letters are sorted again into a new order

parts.note: a rant is bombastic, ranting speech

explanation.surface: A roaming bear starts to shout and bluster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resorting', read as re-sorting, turns BEAR into ABER; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Straying from the normal path, deviating from what is usual.

clue.text: They lack co-ordination, these problem children

indicators.note: the letters lack order and must be co-ordinated, arranged anew

explanation.surface: Clumsy youngsters who cannot co-ordinate their limbs give their parents trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'co-ordination' rearranges THEY LACK. Latchkey children let themselves into empty homes after school because their parents are out at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Children left alone at home carry their own door key, a recognised social worry.

clue.text: Jocular clergyman in the jet set?

definitions.meaning: a slang name for a chaplain, guiding souls heavenward
literally an aviator flying a jet through the heavens

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a padre or chaplain, and literally a pilot who flies through the heavens.

clue.text: Famous old jurist much revered in Mecca

definitions.meaning: Sir William, the 18th-century English legal writer of the Commentaries on the Laws of England
the sacred dark rock set in the corner of the Kaaba, kissed by pilgrims

explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the great English legal commentator also names the sacred relic set in the Kaaba wall.

clue.text: A white man conspicuous in negro society

definitions.text: A white man conspicuous in negro society

parts.words: A white man conspicuous in negro society
parts.note: describes a person of any race born without skin pigment, who stands out among dark-skinned people

explanation.definitionFit: A person lacking natural pigment has very pale skin and hair, standing out among dark-skinned people.

clue.text: What one tries to do to the best of one's ability?

definitions.text: What one tries to do to the best of one's ability?

parts.words: What one tries to do to the best of one's ability?
parts.note: plays on the idiom of doing one's very best, the greatest effort possible

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'do one's ___' means trying as hard as one possibly can.

clue.text: Stealthy prowler, one that thinks about nothing but catching vermin

indicators.note: the thinker's letters go around another piece

parts.note: a muser is someone who muses, that is thinks or ponders
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A creeping hunter that has no thought for anything except catching rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts O inside MUSER; 'but catching vermin' completes the picture of a cat that catches mice.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat that hunts mice stalks its prey silently.

clue.text: Kitchener's formula for success?

parts.note: Kitchener suggests the First World War field marshal, but here means a cook, whose instructions for a dish are a formula for success

explanation.walkthrough: Lord Kitchener was the British war minister of the First World War; here the word just means someone working in a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooking instructions are a set of directions for making a dish turn out well.

clue.text: Titles switched to a point that can be very dangerous

definitions.text: a point that can be very dangerous

indicators.note: the letters of the word are switched around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone swaps the titles round to make a risky argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'switched' makes STILET, a variant spelling of the dagger's name, before the plain 'to'; 'point' seems to be an argument but is the blade's tip.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin, sharp dagger, a pointed blade that can wound badly.

clue.text: A base from which we walk a little way

indicators.note: the letters are taken from inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A starting point from which we set out on a short stroll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A base' looks like a starting point for a walk, but it is the chemical sense; the letters run across walk a little.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry a soluble base, the opposite of an acid, is the term needed.

clue.text: Is roused anew and found wanting?

indicators.note: the letters are put together again in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone is stirred up all over again and found lacking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anew' turns IS ROUSED into the answer; 'found' is a link. 'wanting' looks like 'lacking' but means longing.
explanation.definitionFit: Eager or longing for something, the sense of wanting as desiring.

clue.text: Secret arrangements for meetings, possibly

parts.note: describes private appointments, typically between lovers, agreed in advance

explanation.definitionFit: Lovers' private appointments are arranged meetings kept secret from others.

clue.text: He falsely claims I'm after foreign gold

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
post is the Latin word for after
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A confidence trickster says he is chasing gold abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraud pretends to be someone else, making false claims about identity.
